Description: Detected a Generic API Key, potentially exposing access to various services and sensitive operations.
Author: Sanjar
Message:
feat(api): authentication — argon2, pinned JWT, refresh rotation and reuse detection (#3)

* feat(api): authentication — argon2, pinned JWT, refresh rotation and reuse detection

Registration and login (FR-1, FR-2)
- Argon2id at OWASP's m=19456, t=2, p=1. The test reads those back out of the
  PHC string rather than from the constant the code passes, because asserting
  a value against itself proves nothing.
- `verifySecret` returns false on a malformed digest instead of throwing. That
  case is real: the SYSTEM account's passwordHash is a sentinel (§9.4), and a
  login attempt against it must be an ordinary failure rather than a 500 that
  tells the caller they found something unusual.
- Registration creates the user and their UZS account in one transaction, and
  catches the uniqueness violation rather than pre-checking it — a SELECT then
  INSERT has a window where two concurrent registrations both see the number
  as free. Every rejection returns the identical generic body (FR-1.5).
- Login spends the same time whether or not the number exists, by verifying
  against a pre-computed throwaway digest. Returning early is the natural way
  to write this and it is exactly what S-5 tests for: argon2 at m=19456 takes
  tens of milliseconds, so the fast path would be audible. The digest is
  computed once at startup, not per request, which would be a free DoS lever.

Tokens (FR-2.4 to FR-2.7)
- `jose` rather than `jsonwebtoken`: zero dependencies against ten, six of them
  lodash micro-packages. For the library guarding authentication that decides
  it. It also refuses to verify without an explicit algorithm list.
- HS256 is pinned in both directions, and issuer and audience are checked, so a
  token minted for another service cannot be replayed here. Tests forge
  `alg: none` and `alg: HS512` and watch both fail.
- JWT_SECRET is rejected below 32 characters at boot. A short secret is not
  "weaker but working" — it is the only thing between a forged token and an
  authenticated request, and a deploy using `changeme` would look identical to
  a correct one.
- Refresh tokens are opaque 256-bit values stored as SHA-256 digests (§9.2), not
  JWTs: revocation needs the database anyway, so signing would add risk and
  nothing else (§21 Q-5). SHA-256 rather than Argon2 because the input is our
  own randomness — there is nothing to brute-force and no reason to pay Argon2
  on the hot refresh path.
- Rotation and reuse detection: a token that has already been exchanged coming
  back means either the client replayed it or someone else holds a copy. We
  cannot tell which, so the whole family is revoked and every device signs in
  again. S-4 asserts that the *legitimate* device is signed out too, not only
  the replayed token.

Response validation (T-3.8)
- `respond()` serialises every success through a Zod schema. The shared
  `auth.ts` comment claims a Prisma record parsed through `publicUserSchema`
  has its hash stripped; this is the thing that does the parsing, so the
  guarantee is structural rather than a promise. Forgetting a field now shows
  up as a missing field rather than an invisible leak.

Cookies (FR-2.4)
- httpOnly, SameSite=Strict, Secure outside development, 30 days, scoped to
  /api/auth. Read with a ten-line parser rather than cookie-parser: the only
  cookie this service reads holds a base64url value of our own making, so none
  of the escaping cases that justify the dependency can arise. The comment says
  to use the library if that ever stops being true.

Also
- Verified before adopting: argon2 loads with Yarn's build scripts disabled,
  because node-gyp-build resolves a prebuilt binary at require time.
- Tests build the app through one helper that calls `createApp` exactly as
  index.ts does. The day 2 review found three defects that survived because
  every test assembled its own middleware stack.

Refs runbook T-3.1 to T-3.8; FR-1, FR-2, NFR-1.1, NFR-1.2, NFR-1.4, NFR-1.5,
NFR-1.6; S-4, S-5.

* fix(api): close the auth defects two reviews found

Two independent reviewers ran the properties rather than reading the code, and
found that the tests certified controls they could not detect the loss of.

Refresh reuse detection was bypassable by concurrency
- `refresh()` read `usedAt` and then wrote it unconditionally: a lost update.
  Two replays of one stolen token arriving *together* both read null, both
  wrote, and both got a working session. Reproduced at 4 of 4 accepted, and
  9 of 10 in a second reviewer's harness. Sequential replay — the interleaving
  S-4 tested — is the one an attacker has no reason to choose.
- The claim is now `updateMany` with `usedAt: null` in the predicate, so the
  database arbitrates: the second writer blocks, re-evaluates against the
  committed row, and matches nothing. Family revocation happens after the
  transaction commits, because revoking inside it and then throwing would roll
  the revocation back.
- A concurrent-replay test now exists. Without the predicate it reports
  "accepted 4 of 4"; with it, at most one.

Two timing oracles
- The SYSTEM account answered 3.8x faster than any other number. Its hash is a
  sentinel, not a digest (§9.4), and `verifySecret` caught argon2's throw and
  returned false without spending the CPU — trading a 500 for a far louder
  signal, on the one account that owns the treasury. It now spends the time.
- Login wrote an `AuthAttempt` row only when the number was registered, so a
  known number cost one extra INSERT. Measured at ~6ms and classified numbers
  at 80% accuracy: a working enumeration oracle against FR-2.2 and NFR-1.2.
  `AuthAttempt.userId` is now nullable and the row is written either way,
  which is also what §11.2 draws.
- Both are covered by tests comparing the *minimum* of interleaved samples
  against a ratio bound rather than a median against a millisecond budget.

The S-5 test could not detect its own regression
- The old assertion was `delta < 50ms`. One argon2 verify at m=19456 costs
  ~40ms here, so the naive early-return leak the test's own comment describes
  measured 5ms against 45ms — an 8x separation — and passed. A reviewer
  reproduced it passing 4 times in 9. §18.2's criterion is amended to a ratio,
  because an absolute bound has to be chosen relative to the effect it is
  meant to detect.

A database outage was reported as the user's fault
- `register` caught everything and returned `REGISTRATION_FAILED`. FR-1.5
  requires that only for a taken number; a P1001 became a permanently
  non-retryable 400 telling the user to check their details, with no
  error-level log line anywhere. Now only P2002 is caught.

Contract corrections
- `AUTH_REFRESH_INVALID` added. Answering a failed refresh with
  `AUTH_TOKEN_EXPIRED` tells the client to refresh — the call that just
  failed — which is a loop. §12.3 gains the code and a note on the old one.
- Login no longer enforces the password *minimum*. Reusing `passwordSchema`
  gave the endpoint a third response shape, contradicting FR-2.2's "always
  identical", short-circuiting before any hash work, and it would have locked
  existing accounts out at login the day the policy is raised.
- §12.1 marked `/auth/logout` as bearer-authenticated; it acts on the cookie,
  which is correct — you must be able to log out with an expired access token.
  The table now says so.
- §14's B2 scope named lockout while runbook §4 defers it. Resolved in favour
  of the runbook, with the reason recorded: `AuthAttempt` rows are written from
  day 3 so the counter has history when FR-2.3 lands.
- FR-2.7 now bounds the revocation window. Access tokens are self-contained and
  survive family revocation for up to 15 minutes; that belonged in the spec,
  not in a source comment.

Tests that named a property without checking it
- `respond()` was a no-op across the entire suite — every call site handed it a
  pre-narrowed object, so deleting it left 54/54 green. It now has tests that
  hand it a full Prisma row, and `/health` goes through it too, so "every
  response leaves through here" is true.
- Rotation never replayed the old token; the digest test would have passed for
  a reversible hex encoding; the cookie's `Secure` and `Path` attributes were
  never asserted; an expired refresh token was accepted forever. All four
  mutations were verified to fail the suite now.
- `expiresIn` was asserted against the constant the module exports; it now
  decodes the signed token's own `exp` and `iat`.

Also
- `warmDummyHash()` at startup, so the first unknown-number login after a cold
  start does not pay an extra argon2 hash — a leak in the other direction, and
  Render's free tier makes cold starts routine.
- `safeEqual` removed: exported, called from nowhere, and dead code in a crypto
  module invites a reader to assume something depends on it.
- `CORS_ORIGINS` is marked as not yet consumed. It still fails boot in
  production, deliberately, so a deploy cannot reach B5 without it.

Five findings are parked with reasons in docs/PARKING.md. The two worth
knowing: registration has the same timing oracle as login and closing it needs
a response-padding decision, and `SameSite=Strict` cannot work across Vercel
and Render, so refresh will pass every test here and fail on first deploy.

Refs FR-1.5, FR-2.2, FR-2.4, FR-2.6, FR-2.7, NFR-1.2, NFR-5.1; §11.2, §12.1,
§12.3, §14, §18.2 S-4 and S-5.

* fix(api): seeding needs a connection string, not the whole environment

`seed()` called `loadEnv()`, which validates every variable including
JWT_SECRET — so the script refused to run without a secret it never uses, and
CI failed on the one test that seeds the treasury. It now takes an optional
client, and closes only the connection it opened rather than a caller's.

CI also gains a JWT_SECRET. The API refuses to boot without one (NFR-1.9), so
the integration tests need it; it is job-scoped and ephemeral like the database
credentials beside it.

Verified by running the suite with the local .env removed and only the two
variables CI supplies: 61 passed.
